subject: Social Science — Geography
textbook: Our Environment — Textbook for Class VI

cards.front: What are Earth's two main motions? Give the time period for each.
cards.back: 1. Rotation: Earth spinning on its own axis. Period = 24 hours (one solar day). 2. Revolution: Earth orbiting the Sun. Period = 365.25 days (one year). Both motions happen simultaneously — while Earth orbits the Sun (revolution), it is also continuously spinning on its axis (rotation). These two independent motions together create our experience of days, nights, and seasons.
cards.memory_hook: Rotation = spinning like a top (daily). Revolution = going around the Sun (yearly). Two R's, two motions, two different time scales. R-daily, R-yearly. ROT = daily, REV = yearly.

cards.front: In which direction does Earth rotate? What is the consequence for the Sun's apparent movement?
cards.back: Earth rotates from west to east (counterclockwise when viewed from above the North Pole). Consequence: because Earth rotates west-to-east, an observer on Earth sees the Sun appear to move in the opposite direction — east to west. This is why the Sun 'rises' in the east (Earth's surface rotates into the Sun's light from the east side) and 'sets' in the west (rotates away from it on the west side). The Sun is not actually moving — it is Earth rotating that creates this apparent daily motion.
cards.memory_hook: Earth spins W→E. Sun APPEARS to go E→W. They're opposites! Think: if you walk forward (east), everything outside appears to go backward (west). Earth walks east; Sun appears to walk west. Action and appearance are always opposite.

cards.front: How does rotation cause day and night?
cards.back: Earth is a sphere. The Sun can only illuminate one half of Earth at a time — the half facing the Sun. The illuminated half = DAY. The half facing away from the Sun = NIGHT. As Earth rotates (west to east), different parts of Earth come into and out of sunlight. A complete rotation (360°) takes 24 hours. So every location on Earth experiences approximately 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night (varying slightly with season). The boundary between the lit and dark sides is called the circle of illumination.
cards.memory_hook: Earth = a spinning ball in a spotlight. Half is always lit (day), half always dark (night). Rotate the ball — the lit part shifts. Day and night = the spotlight hitting different parts of the ball as it spins. Simple. Beautiful.

cards.front: What is revolution? How long does Earth take to complete one revolution?
cards.back: Revolution is Earth's orbital motion around the Sun. Earth travels in a slightly elliptical (oval-shaped) path around the Sun, completing one full orbit in approximately 365.25 days = one year. The extra 0.25 days accumulate over 4 years to equal 1 full day, which is added as February 29 in a Leap Year (366 days). Earth's closest point to the Sun is called perihelion (~147 million km, in January); farthest point is aphelion (~152 million km, in July). Importantly, this distance change does NOT cause seasons.
cards.memory_hook: Revolution = going around the Sun like revolving doors. 365.25 days = 1 year. 0.25 × 4 = 1 extra day every 4 years = Leap Year. The extra day goes to February — the shortest month gets a bonus day every 4 years.

cards.front: What causes seasons? Why is Earth's distance from the Sun NOT the cause?
cards.back: Seasons are caused ONLY by Earth's axial tilt of 23.5°. As Earth revolves, the tilted axis means different hemispheres receive more direct and prolonged sunlight at different times of year — that hemisphere experiences summer. The other hemisphere, receiving less direct/prolonged sunlight, experiences winter. Earth's distance from the Sun is NOT the cause because: Earth is actually CLOSEST to the Sun in January (perihelion) — which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere! If distance were the cause, January would be the hottest month, not the coldest.
cards.memory_hook: Seasons = TILT. Period. Earth is closest to Sun in JANUARY (N. Hemisphere winter) — prove distance does NOT cause seasons. The 23.5° tilt makes some regions receive more direct, longer sunlight = summer. Less direct, shorter sunlight = winter. Angle of light matters, not distance.

cards.front: What is Earth's axial tilt? Why does it remain constant in direction?
cards.back: Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane (from the vertical, relative to its orbit around the Sun). This tilt remains constant in direction throughout the year — the North Pole always points towards the same spot in space, near Polaris (the Pole Star / North Star). This constant direction is called axial parallelism or parallelism of the axis. Because the tilt is constant and the direction is fixed, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in June (summer) and away from the Sun in December (winter) — creating the seasonal pattern.
cards.memory_hook: Earth's axis = a stubborn pointer — always tilted the same way, always pointing towards Polaris. It doesn't wobble as Earth orbits the Sun (on human timescales). This stubbornness + the changing orbital position = seasons. If the axis tilted freely, there would be no seasons.

cards.front: What is the Summer Solstice? When does it occur in the Northern Hemisphere?
cards.back: The Summer Solstice is the day when the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most towards the Sun — it is the longest day (maximum daylight hours) of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. Date: June 21. On this day: the Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N). Northern Hemisphere has its longest day. Above the Arctic Circle (66.5°N) — 24 hours of daylight (midnight sun). Below the Antarctic Circle (66.5°S) — 24 hours of darkness. The Southern Hemisphere experiences its winter solstice simultaneously.
cards.memory_hook: June 21 = N. Hemisphere Summer Solstice = longest day. Sun directly over Cancer (23.5°N). 'JUN-gle heat' → June → Summer → Cancer → North. In Norway, the sun never sets. In Antarctica, the sun never rises. Earth is most 'lopsided' in terms of light distribution on this day.

cards.front: What is the Winter Solstice? When does it occur in the Northern Hemisphere?
cards.back: The Winter Solstice is the day when the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most away from the Sun — the shortest day (minimum daylight hours) of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. Date: December 22. On this day: the Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S). Northern Hemisphere has its shortest day. Above the Arctic Circle — 24 hours of darkness (polar night). Below the Antarctic Circle — 24 hours of daylight. The Southern Hemisphere experiences its summer solstice simultaneously. Uttarayan (Makar Sankranti) in India celebrates the return of sunlight after this date.
cards.memory_hook: December 22 = N. Hemisphere Winter Solstice = shortest day. Sun directly over Capricorn (23.5°S). 'DeCember Cold' → December → Winter → Capricorn → South. After Dec 22, days start getting longer in the Northern Hemisphere — that's what Uttarayan/Sankranti celebrates.

cards.front: What are equinoxes? When do they occur?
cards.back: Equinoxes are the two days per year when Earth's axis is neither tilted towards nor away from the Sun — the Sun shines directly on the Equator, and day and night are equal (12 hours each) everywhere on Earth. Spring (Vernal) Equinox: March 21 — start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere. Autumnal Equinox: September 23 — start of autumn in the Northern Hemisphere. The word 'equinox' comes from Latin: equi = equal, nox = night. 'Equal night' — both halves of Earth receive equal sunlight.
cards.memory_hook: EQUIlibrium NIGHT = EQUINOX. March 21 and September 23. Equal day and night EVERYWHERE on Earth on these two days. Sun shines directly on the Equator. 'March 21 = fair share day — everyone gets exactly 12 hours of sun.' Ugadi (Karnataka) celebrates near March equinox.

cards.front: When India experiences summer, what season does Australia experience? Why?
cards.back: When India (Northern Hemisphere) experiences summer (approximately April–June), Australia (Southern Hemisphere) experiences autumn/winter. This is because of Earth's axial tilt: when the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun (India's summer, June 21 being the peak), the Southern Hemisphere is simultaneously tilted away from the Sun — giving Australia less sunlight, lower temperatures, and winter conditions. The hemispheres ALWAYS have opposite seasons. The only exceptions are equinoxes (March 21, September 23) when neither hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun.
cards.memory_hook: India summer = Australia winter. Always opposite, always. Think of a see-saw: when one side goes up (summer, towards Sun), the other goes down (winter, away from Sun). Hemispheres are on a permanent seasonal see-saw controlled by Earth's orbital position.

cards.front: What is a Leap Year? Why is it needed?
cards.back: A Leap Year is a year with 366 days — February has 29 days instead of 28. It occurs every 4 years. Why needed: Earth takes exactly 365.25 days to orbit the Sun. Calendar years have only 365 days. After 4 years, 4 × 0.25 = 1 full extra day has accumulated. Adding this day (February 29) every 4th year keeps the calendar aligned with Earth's orbital position. Without Leap Years, the calendar would shift by 1 day every 4 years — after 100 years, the seasons would be off by 25 days. Examples of Leap Years: 2020, 2024, 2028. Rule: divisible by 4 (with exceptions for century years).
cards.memory_hook: Leap Year = the calendar's correction day. Earth is 1/4 day late every year. After 4 years, it owes us a full day. We collect on February 29. 2024 was a Leap Year — 2028 will be next. 365.25 × 4 = 1461 days = 4 years + 1 day.

cards.front: On the Summer Solstice (June 21), what does someone in Chennai experience vs someone in Oslo (above Arctic Circle)?
cards.back: Chennai (~13°N, tropical zone): On June 21, daylight is slightly longer than night (about 13 hours of daylight). The Sun rises high in the sky but is not directly overhead (Chennai is south of the Tropic of Cancer at 23.5°N). Chennai is in the early monsoon period — hot and humid with the onset of SW Monsoon. Oslo (~60°N, near Arctic Circle): On June 21, Oslo experiences very long days — approximately 19–20 hours of daylight. The Sun barely sets, remaining low on the horizon even at midnight (near midnight sun). This dramatic contrast shows how the Summer Solstice affects different latitudes very differently.
cards.memory_hook: Same planet, same date, same June 21 — completely different experience. Chennai gets 13 hours of day; Oslo gets 20 hours. Latitude determines how extreme the season feels. Near the Equator = gentle seasons. Near the poles = extreme seasons. The tropics barely notice solstices; the poles are dominated by them.

cards.front: How do Karnataka's monsoon seasons relate to Earth's revolution and axial tilt?
cards.back: Karnataka's Southwest Monsoon (June–September) is directly caused by the combination of Earth's revolution and axial tilt: As Earth revolves to its June position (Northern Hemisphere summer solstice), the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. This intense heating of the Asian landmass creates a powerful low-pressure zone over Central Asia and India. The ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) shifts northward. Moisture-laden winds from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal are drawn north — this is the Southwest Monsoon. The monsoon ends in September as Earth continues revolving and the Sun moves southward again. Karnataka's kharif crop (paddy, ragi, jowar) is timed to the monsoon — itself timed to Earth's orbital calendar.
cards.memory_hook: Monsoon = Earth's summer tilt + Sun over Asia = low pressure = moisture pulled from ocean = RAIN over Karnataka. Every raindrop in the Karnataka monsoon began with Earth tilting its Northern Hemisphere towards the Sun. Orbital mechanics → atmospheric circulation → rain → Karnataka paddy fields.

cards.front: Why does Karnataka celebrate Ugadi around March and Makar Sankranti in January?
cards.back: Ugadi (March–April): Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh's New Year is celebrated near the Spring Equinox (March 21) — the day of equal day and night that marks the beginning of spring and the renewal of the agricultural year. The equinox signals increasing daylight, warming temperatures, and the start of a new agricultural cycle — hence, the new year. Makar Sankranti (January 14): Celebrates the Sun's apparent northward movement (Uttarayan) after the Winter Solstice (December 22). 'Makar' = Capricorn (Sanskrit), 'Sankranti' = transition. The Sun transitions from Sagittarius to Capricorn (in the zodiac) — marking the end of the dark period and the return of increasing daylight. Both festivals are ancient astronomical observations encoded in cultural celebration.
cards.memory_hook: Ugadi = Spring Equinox festival (March — equal day/night, new beginning). Sankranti = Solstice transition festival (January — Sun turns north again after December 22). Ancient Indians were excellent astronomers — their festival calendar is literally a celebration of Earth's orbital milestones.

cards.front: What is the circle of illumination?
cards.back: The circle of illumination is the boundary between the illuminated (day) half and the dark (night) half of Earth at any given moment. It is a great circle that divides Earth into two equal halves — one facing the Sun (daytime) and one facing away (nighttime). As Earth rotates, the circle of illumination appears to sweep across Earth's surface from east to west — bringing sunrise to new longitudes and sunset to others. On the equinoxes, the circle of illumination passes through both the North and South Poles exactly, giving equal day and night to all latitudes.
cards.memory_hook: Circle of illumination = the day/night dividing line on a spinning Earth. Imagine Earth as a hard-boiled egg cut in half — one half lit, one half dark. As the egg spins (rotation), different parts move into and out of the lit half. That dividing cut = circle of illumination.

cards.front: Why does ISRO prefer to launch satellites from a low latitude site like Sriharikota (13.7°N)?
cards.back: Earth's surface rotates faster at the Equator and slower at the poles. At the Equator, the surface moves at ~1,670 km/h (Earth's equatorial circumference ÷ 24 hours). At Sriharikota (13.7°N), the surface moves at ~1,624 km/h. This rotational velocity is 'free' extra speed given to any eastward rocket launch — it reduces the fuel needed to achieve orbital velocity. By contrast, launching from a polar location would provide no such benefit. Most space agencies (NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 28.5°N, ESA's Kourou in French Guiana at 5.2°N) also choose low-latitude launch sites for this reason.
cards.memory_hook: Low latitude = Earth spinning faster = free speed boost for rockets. The Earth is like a slingshot — standing near the Equator and launching east means Earth's rotation throws you forward. ISRO's choice of Sriharikota at 13.7°N is a calculated use of Earth's rotation for fuel efficiency.

cards.front: What would happen if Earth had no axial tilt?
cards.back: If Earth's axis were perfectly upright (0° tilt, perpendicular to its orbital plane), there would be NO seasons. Every location on Earth would receive the same amount of sunlight year-round — the Equator would always be hottest, the poles always coldest, and no seasonal variation would exist. Day length would be 12 hours everywhere, every day of the year. The Sun would always be directly overhead at the Equator. There would be no solstices or equinoxes. All agriculture would have no planting/harvest seasons. Climate would be static. All the seasonal festivals (Ugadi, Sankranti, Holi, etc.) would have no astronomical basis. The 23.5° tilt is essentially what makes Earth dynamic, diverse, and liveable across its surface.
cards.memory_hook: No tilt = no seasons = no change. Earth would be like a perfectly balanced spinning top — equator always hot, poles always cold, middle zones always the same. Boring! The 23.5° tilt is Earth's gift of diversity — hot summers, cool winters, monsoons, snowfall — all because of a slight lean.

cards.front: On which date and at which latitude is the Sun directly overhead on: (a) June 21, (b) December 22, (c) March 21 and September 23?
cards.back: (a) June 21 — Sun directly overhead at Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N). Summer Solstice in Northern Hemisphere. (b) December 22 — Sun directly overhead at Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S). Winter Solstice in Northern Hemisphere. (c) March 21 and September 23 — Sun directly overhead at the Equator (0°). These are the Equinoxes — equal day and night everywhere. Pattern: The Sun appears to move between 23.5°N (Tropic of Cancer) and 23.5°S (Tropic of Capricorn) over the course of a year — this apparent annual north-south movement is called the apparent annual motion of the Sun.
cards.memory_hook: Four dates, four positions: June 21 → Cancer (23.5°N). December 22 → Capricorn (23.5°S). March 21 and September 23 → Equator (0°). Sun oscillates like a pendulum between Cancer and Capricorn over the year. The Equator gets the Sun on the two 'middle swing' dates.

cards.front: A student in Norway reports 'It is June 21 and the Sun has not set — it has been daylight for 20 hours!' Why?
cards.back: Norway is at approximately 60°N–71°N latitude, partially above the Arctic Circle (66.5°N). On June 21 (Summer Solstice), the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most towards the Sun. At 66.5°N and above, the Sun does not set at all — 24 hours of daylight (midnight sun). Even at 60°N (Oslo), the Sun barely dips below the horizon, giving near-continuous daylight (~20 hours). This is because on June 21, the circle of illumination reaches as far south as 66.5°S (Antarctic Circle) — meaning the entire region from 66.5°N to 90°N (North Pole) is continuously in sunlight. The Northern Hemisphere's maximum tilt towards the Sun is the direct cause.
cards.memory_hook: Midnight sun = June 21 above Arctic Circle. Same reason Karnataka gets its monsoon (sun is overhead in the north) — it is the same orbital event creating wildly different experiences: Norway gets no night while Karnataka gets flooded. One tilt, infinite consequences.

cards.front: Summarise the four seasons in the Northern Hemisphere, their approximate dates, and Earth's orbital position.
cards.back: Spring: March 21–June 21. Sun moves from Equator towards Cancer. Northern Hemisphere warming up. Days becoming longer. Summer: June 21–September 23. Sun between Cancer and Equator. Hottest period. Longest days. Monsoon in India. Autumn: September 23–December 22. Sun moves from Equator towards Capricorn. Cooling down. Days getting shorter. Winter: December 22–March 21. Sun between Capricorn and Equator. Coldest period. Shortest days. Northern Hemisphere tilted away from Sun. Note: Karnataka, being tropical, does not experience the classic four seasons as sharply as temperate countries, but has Hot (March–May), Monsoon (June–September), Post-Monsoon (October–November), and Cool (December–February) seasons.
cards.memory_hook: Four seasons = four quadrants of Earth's orbit. Spring equinox → Summer solstice → Autumn equinox → Winter solstice → back to Spring. Four orbital milestones divide the year into four seasons. Karnataka's version: Hot → Wet (Monsoon) → Cool-Wet → Cool-Dry.
